title: Count Valid Suffix Sorts II
solution: Let A_i = nums[0..i-1] followed by nums[i..n-1] sorted non-increasingly, and W_k = target[k..k+n-1]. A_i == W_k iff (a) nums[0..i-1] == W_k[0..i-1], i.e. i <= L_k, the longest common prefix of nums and target[k..] (capped at n); (b) W_k[i..] is non-increasing, i.e. i >= S_k, where S_k is where the maximal non-increasing run of target ending at k+n-1 starts (clamped to the window); and (c) W_k[i..] and nums[i..] are the same multiset, which given (a) is equivalent to W_k being a permutation (anagram) of all of nums. (a) and (b) are monotone in i in opposite directions, so ans[k] = max(0, min(L_k, n-1) - S_k + 1) when (c) holds and 0 otherwise. All L_k come from one Z-function pass over nums + [separator] + target; S_k from a left-to-right run array over target (run[j] = run[j-1] if target[j-1] >= target[j] else j); (c) from a fixed-length sliding window over target maintaining a frequency-difference count array against nums (values <= 1e5) and the number of non-zero entries. Total O(n + m + V) time for n <= m <= 1e5. Equivalent alternatives: compute L_k by binary search on polynomial prefix hashes (O(m log n)), or skip the interval argument entirely and hash every A_i (prefix hash of nums[0..i-1] times B^(n-i) plus the hash of the sorted multiset kept in a segment tree indexed by value in descending order, inserting nums[i] as i goes from n-1 down to 0), store hash -> count in a hash map, and roll a hash over every window of target, O((n + m) log V).

solution_check.how: Python sol.py (Z-function + run array + sliding frequency-difference window) matches both statement examples ([1,1,0,0,0,1] and [2,1,0,2]) and, with m = n, all 3 examples of sibling I (1, 2, 0). Brute force builds nums[:i] + sorted(nums[i:], reverse=True) for every i and compares to every window. Stress: 30,000 cases with n in 1..7, m in n..14, values 1..V (V in 1..4), targets half spliced from real suffix-sort outputs (26,736 had a nonzero answer), plus 5,000 cases with n in 1..30, m up to 70, values 1..3 (66,205 nonzero windows); all agreed. alt_hash.py: two hashing alternatives (prefix-hash + binary-search LCP; full hash of every A_i via a value-indexed segment tree + rolling hash over windows + hash-map counts) agree with brute force and the Z solution on 20,000 random cases and the examples. Timing: n = m = 1e5 in 0.03 s; full-hash variant n = 5e4, m = 1e5 in 0.23 s.

rejected_patterns.reason: This names one alternative twice. rolling-hash and string-hashing both stand for polynomial hashing of nums and target, and that hashing is a substitute for the Z-function LCP, not a second idea. Only one hashing label should stay. I kept rolling-hash for three reasons. First, the corpus's LeetCode prefix-hash and LCP precedents use rolling-hash, not string-hashing: leetcode-sum-of-scores-of-built-strings (the closest analog, LCP of a string at every offset: z-function + rolling-hash + string-matching), longest-happy-prefix, shortest-palindrome and repeated-string-match. Second, the taxonomy aliases the generic query 'hashing' to rolling-hash. Third, LeetCode's own topic tag is 'Rolling Hash'.

notes.solver: z-function: n <= m forces the longest common prefix of nums with every offset of target, which is exactly one Z-function pass over nums + sep + target; this is what separates II from I (where n == m and a single forward scan suffices). sliding-window: condition (c) is a fixed-length anagram window over target, maintained in O(1) per step with a frequency-difference array and a non-zero counter. string-matching: the problem is matching a family of n arrays derived from nums against every window of target, solved with a linear pattern-matching algorithm (LeetCode-style 'String Matching' tag). counting: the multiset test is a frequency count comparison (kept for consistency with sibling I's labels). rolling-hash / string-hashing (0.5 each): genuine verified alternatives, the LCP by binary search on polynomial prefix hashes, or hashing each distinct A_i and rolling a hash over target windows with hash -> count lookups; 'hashing' queries alias to rolling-hash, 'polynomial hashing' to string-hashing. Rejected: kmp (prefix function gives prefixes ending at a text position, not the LCP starting at each offset, so it does not directly give L_k), sorting (the statement's word; no solution sorts a suffix), segment-tree (only inside the heavier full-hash alternative, to maintain the hash of a sorted multiset; not what anyone would search this problem for), hash-map as a pattern (values <= 1e5 so a count array suffices; left as a tag), two-pointers / monotonic-stack (the non-increasing run is a one-line linear scan, scaffolding), prefix-sum (no range sums), binary-search / binary-search-answer (the interval bounds are read directly; binary search appears only inside the hashing LCP variant as an LCP lookup, not as a technique a searcher wants), greedy, brute-force (O(n * m) comparisons do not fit 1e5).
notes.skeptic:
SOLUTION. A_i = nums[0..i-1] + sortdesc(nums[i..]) equals the window W_k exactly when three things hold. (a) i <= L_k, the LCP of nums and target[k..]. (b) W_k[i..] is non-increasing, i.e. i >= run[k+n-1]-k. (c) The multisets of nums[i..] and W_k[i..] agree, which given (a) is the same as W_k being an anagram of the whole of nums. (a) is downward-closed in i and (b) is upward-closed, so the valid i form the interval [max(0, run-k), min(L_k, n-1)]. The proposal's algorithm, proof and complexity are correct. My independent implementation and the solver's three implementations all match brute force.

PATTERNS.
z-function: KEEP (0.95). Computing the LCP of nums with every offset of target is the textbook Z-array use. It is what separates II (n <= m) from I (n == m, one forward scan). KMP / prefix-function is NOT the natural tool. pi gives the longest prefix of nums that ENDS at each text position, but L_k needs the longest prefix that STARTS at k, and getting it from pi means walking border chains or a pi-to-z conversion. I agree with rejecting kmp.
sliding-window: KEEP (0.85). Condition (c) does not obviously reduce to a fixed-length anagram window over target. Once it does, the window is maintained in O(1) per step with a frequency-difference array and a non-zero counter. That is a real step, not scaffolding: dropping it gives wrong answers. Example: nums=[1], target=[2] has L=0 and run start 0 but the answer is 0. Precedent is leetcode-permutation-in-string, also sliding-window + counting.
counting: KEEP (0.65). The window's contents are the frequency table, and the multiset-equality test carries correctness. Sibling I's review kept counting as its only pattern for the same test, and the taxonomy aliases frequency-count, frequency-array and frequency-counting to counting. It is not the label for 'the answer is a count', which would be statement echo. Confidence is moderate because it overlaps with sliding-window.
string-matching: KEEP (0.6). This is a pattern-against-every-offset matching problem over integer arrays. The taxonomy has no family rule from z-function to string-matching, so the family query 'pattern matching' / 'substring search' (both aliased to string-matching) only reaches this record if the label is explicit. Precedents: leetcode-number-of-subarrays-that-match-a-pattern-ii (integer arrays) and leetcode-sum-of-scores-of-built-strings.
rolling-hash: KEEP (0.5) as the one hashing label. Computing L_k by binary search on polynomial prefix hashes is a common contest alternative to Z for LCP at every offset, and the solver verified it (alt_hash.py, which I re-ran). It earns a place because a 'hashing' search should reach this problem. It stays at 0.5 because it is a substitute route, not the intended one.
string-hashing: REJECT. It duplicates rolling-hash (see rejected_patterns).

MISSING LABELS CONSIDERED, NONE ADDED. kmp: see above. suffix-array: suffix array + LCP + RMQ also gives L_k, but nobody would write it for one pattern against one text. randomized-algorithm: a random-weight multiset hash could replace the count window, but the count array is simpler and exact. two-pointers / monotonic-stack: the non-increasing run array is a one-line scan, i.e. scaffolding. sorting: the statement's own verb, and no solution sorts. binary-search: appears only inside the hash-LCP variant as a lookup. prefix-sum, greedy and brute-force do not apply (O(nm) does not fit 1e5). segment-tree: appears only in the heavier full-hash variant.

TRAP 1, binary-search-answer: does not apply. The answer is a count per window, not an optimum with a feasibility test. Both interval bounds are read directly from the Z-array and the run array. The only binary search anywhere is the LCP-length lookup inside the hashing alternative. That search is over a monotone 'prefix matches' predicate, and the predicate is a hash comparison, not an interesting feasibility check, so it is not binary-search-answer under the corpus definition.
TRAP 2, the bitmask-dp vs interval-DP kind of near-miss: there is no DP here. The analogous trap is the constraint split between siblings. I (n == m) has one alignment and needs only counting. II (n <= m <= 1e5) needs the LCP at every offset and an anagram test on every window, so it gets z-function and sliding-window. Labelling the two identically would be the careless-annotator error. The second near-miss is z-function vs kmp, decided by starts-at vs ends-at. The third is rolling-hash vs string-hashing, which are synonyms here, so only one is kept.

SUMMARY. The proposal's summary was accurate, 67 words, and stated the constraint and the reduction. I rewrote it so that it names which side bounds the interval (the LCP caps it, the non-increasing tail floors it), says what the LCP is between, and names the frequency-count window explicitly. The result is 69 words.

TAGS. I kept them as proposed. 'string' is justified by the string-algorithm core and the integer-array pattern-match precedent, which carries a 'string' tag. hash-map stays as a tag only, the same as in sibling I.
